lessons.title: друг (drug) — "friend," the word that explains why ты exists
lessons.gloss: friend (male, or unspecified) — masculine, and the reason you own ты at all

segments.text: A new chapter, and the first word in it names exactly who Chapter 2's informal ты was built for.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — друг

segments.text: друг — drug — friend (a man, or a friend generally).

Consonant-final, so masculine — the ending rule holding steady for the third time. Every letter is one you already read — none of them the throat-rasp х that хлеб just taught you; that one waits for a later word.

(Romanized, this word is spelled exactly like the English drug — pure accident of transliteration, no shared root at all. Say it drook-ish, not like the English word it happens to resemble on the page.)

This is the noun Chapter 2's whole ты/вы choice was about. Ты is for a друг (drug) — someone close enough that formality would feel wrong. Вы is for the stranger, the elder, the shopkeeper: everyone друг (drug) does not cover.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — loyalty, not the modern English you'd expect

segments.text: друг (drug) is Indo-European dʰrewgʰ-, "to accompany, to be loyal" — a companion-on-the-road sense, not far from друг (drug)'s meaning today. Its clearest descendants sit outside everyday modern English: Gothic gadrauhts, "warrior" (literally one who accompanies), and Old English dryhten, "lord" — originally the leader a troop of drauhts followed, a word that survives only in old poetry now, not in ordinary speech.

Unlike хлеб's tidy modern cousin loaf, this is a root that mostly vanished from English rather than one that thrived in it — worth saying plainly rather than stretching for a connection that isn't really there.

segments.text: Say "friend." (Друг.) Which pronoun goes with a друг (drug), and which is for everyone else? (Ты for a friend; вы otherwise.) What did друг (drug)'s root originally mean? (To accompany, to be loyal — Gothic gadrauhts, "warrior"; English dryhten, now archaic.) Is друг (drug) related to the English word it looks like on the page? (No — pure spelling coincidence.) And what English word is хлеб's modern cousin? (Loaf.)

lessons.title: подруга (podrúga) — "friend" (female), built on the word you just learned
lessons.gloss: friend (female) — feminine, and друг with a prefix and an ending stitched on

segments.text: Russian doesn't reach for a new word to make друг (drug) feminine — it builds one, in front of your eyes, out of pieces you already have.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — подруга

segments.text: подруга — podrúga — friend (a woman).
Ends in -а, so feminine — the rule holding for the second time in this chapter, this time on a longer word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: watch the word get built

segments.text: Take друг (drug) apart and put it back together:
по- (a prefix here worn down to little independent meaning) + друг (drug) (friend) + -а (the feminine ending) becomes подруга (podrúga).

This is Russian's ordinary machinery for turning a masculine person-word feminine: keep the root, change the ending, sometimes add a light prefix along the way. It is the same instinct English uses in host becomes host-ess or actor becomes actr-ess — a suffix doing the work — except Russian reaches for this pattern constantly, on ordinary words, not just a formal handful.
Say the pair together and the family resemblance is obvious:
друг, подруга — drug, podrúga.

segments.instruction: "подруга (podrúga)" — feminine, stress on the second syllable

segments.text: Say "friend" for a woman. (Подруга.) What three pieces build it, and what does each contribute? (По- + друг (drug) + -а, the feminine ending.) What English pattern does the same job, on different words? (-ess, as in host/hostess.) And what does друг (drug) itself trace back to? (PIE dʰrewgʰ-, "to accompany, be loyal.")

lessons.title: брат (brat) — "brother," the noun Chapter 5 already warned you about
lessons.gloss: brother — masculine, one soft sign away from a verb you already know, and this time it really is your English cousin

segments.text: Chapter 5 told you брат (brat) meant "brother" and was not related to the verb брать, "to take" — a warning, in passing, about a word not yet properly taught. Here it is, properly taught.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — брат

segments.text: брат — brat — brother. Masculine.

Consonant-final, so the ending rule holds a fourth time. And here is the minimal pair Chapter 5 flagged: брат (brother) against брать (to take, romanized brat') — one soft sign, and nothing else, separates them. Say brat with a hard final t for "brother"; brat' with a soft one for "to take."

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the cognate that actually holds

segments.text: брат (brat) is Indo-European bʰréh₂tēr — and this time the resemblance to English is not a trap but the real thing: brother is the same word, inherited, not borrowed. So is Latin frāter ( becomes fraternal, fraternity), and Sanskrit bhrātar. Few words in any language family are reconstructed with as much confidence as this one.

Recall Chapter 5's other two bʰ- words, because the three sit right next to each other and mean three different things: брать (bʰer-, "to carry" becomes bear, birth), быть (bʰuH-, "to be" becomes English be), and now брат (brat) (bʰréh₂tēr, "brother"). Three roots, one shared opening sound, no shared meaning — a family accent, not a family.

Is брат (brat)'s resemblance to English brother real or a trap? (Real — inherited, like Latin frāter and Sanskrit bhrātar.) Name Chapter 5's two other bʰ- words, and what each one means. (Быть, "to be"; брать, "to take" — three different roots, one shared sound.)

lessons.title: сестра (sestrá) — "sister," and the chapter closes on four people
lessons.gloss: sister — feminine, brat's other half, and a cognate just as secure

segments.text: Брат (brat)'s partner, one more secure cognate, and the four people this chapter has introduced you to, gathered in one place.

blocks.title: You'll want to know first — сестра

segments.text: сестра — sestrá — sister. Feminine.
Ends in -а, stress on the end: ses-TRÁ. Say брат (brat) and сестра (sestrá) together and you have both siblings, both genders' endings, in one breath.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — brother's pair, just as secure

segments.text: сестра (sestrá) is Indo-European swésōr — and, like брат (brat), this is a straight inheritance, not a loan and not a false lead. English sister is the same word (by way of Old Norse, reinforcing an Old English form that had drifted further); Latin's version, soror, took a bumpier sound-change road to the same root. Brother and sister arrive as a matched pair in Russian exactly as they do in the deep history of the whole family.

Chapter 2 gave you ты for someone close and вы for everyone else — the same choice English used to make with thou and you, before thou died out and you took over both jobs. This chapter has now named exactly who sits on the ты side of that line: a друг (drug), a подруга (podrúga), a брат (brat), a сестра (sestrá) — the people close enough that formality would be strange. Everyone else still gets вы.

segments.text: Say "sister," with its gender. (Сестра — feminine.) Is its resemblance to English sister real? (Yes — both from PIE swésōr.) Name all four people this chapter taught, and which pronoun goes with every one of them. (Друг, подруга (podrúga), брат (brat), сестра (sestrá) — all ты.) What pair of English words used to make the same close/distant choice Russian's ты/вы still makes? (Thou and you.)
